speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The U.S. economy expanded at a solid pace last year and is coming into 2026 on a firm footing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: While job gains have remained low, the unemployment rate has shown some signs of stabilization, and inflation remains somewhat elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of our goals, today the Federal Open Market Committee decided to leave our policy rate unchanged.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Having lowered our policy rate by 75 basis points over the course of our previous three meetings, we see the current stance of monetary policy as appropriate to promote progress toward both our maximum-employment and 2 percent inflation goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Available indicators suggest that economic activity has been expanding at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumer spending has been resilient, and business fixed investment has continued to expand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, activity in the housing sector has remained weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The temporary shutdown of the federal government likely weighed on economic activity last quarter, but these effects should be reversed as the reopening boosts growth this quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, indicators suggest that conditions may be stabilizing after a period of gradual softening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate was 4.4 percent in December and has changed little in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job gains have remained low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Total nonfarm payrolls declined at an average pace of 22,000 per month over the last three months; excluding government employment, private payrolls rose at an average pace of 29,000 per month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A good part of the slowing in the pace of job growth over the past year reflects a decline in the growth of the labor force due to lower immigration and labor force participation, though labor demand has clearly softened as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Other indicators, including openings, layoffs, hiring, and nominal wage growth, show little change in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly from its highs in mid-2022 but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.9 percent over the 12 months ending in December and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 3.0 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These elevated readings largely reflect inflation in the goods sector, which has been boosted by the effects of tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, disinflation appears to be continuing in the services sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have declined from last year’s peaks, as reflected in both market- and survey-based measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3½ to 3¾ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Since last September, we have lowered our policy rate 75 basis points, or ¾ of a percentage point, bringing it within a range of plausible estimates of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This normalization of our policy stance should help stabilize the labor market while allowing inflation to resume its downward trend toward 2 percent once the effects of tariff increases have passed through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are well positioned to determine the extent and timing of additional adjustments to our policy rate based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Monetary policy is not on a preset course, and we will make our decisions on a meeting-by-meeting basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To conclude, the Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy: maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will continue to do our jobs with objectivity, integrity, and a deep commitment to serve the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Hi.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Chris Rugaber at Associated Press.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: I wanted to ask—you attended the Supreme Court hearing last week on the Lisa Cook case, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized that as political.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Can you say why you attended and what you would say in response to the secretary’s criticism?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let me start with, I don’t respond to comments by other officials, whoever they may be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just not appropriate to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will tell you why I attended.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say that that case is perhaps the most important legal case in the Fed’s 113-year history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as I thought about it, I thought it might be hard to explain why I didn’t attend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, Paul Volcker went to a Supreme Court case famously in, I guess, 1985 or so, so it’s precedented, and I thought it was an appropriate thing, and I did it.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Great.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: And then just quickly follow on, the job market—you mentioned last month that the household survey might be distorted, and you also mentioned the potential for overcounting jobs, which would suggest that we’re still in a negative hiring pace.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: So do you see the drop in the unemployment rate as solid?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: And I’m just—what’s the basis for saying that things have stabilized?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, yeah, really two questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One is—so we’re getting through the distortions in the data from the shutdown.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What—however big they were in November, they’re smaller in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re getting to a place where they’re no longer material.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re still there, but it’s a tweak here and there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The reason why we—why we changed the statement, let me pull it out, was, was simply, it’s—it used to say that “judges the downside risks to employment rose in recent months.” So we saw data coming in which suggests some signs of stabilization—I wouldn’t go too far with that, but some signs of stabilization.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are also some signs of continued cooling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we thought that was no longer an accurate description of the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, the outlook for economic activity has improved—clearly improved—since the last meeting, and that should matter for labor demand and for employment over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, for those two reasons, we thought we would take that language out of the statement.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nick.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Nick Timiraos, the Wall Street Journal.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Chair Powell, you’ve generally avoided engaging with political controversies directly, and the video statement on January 11 was a departure.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: What made this different, and are you concerned it could draw the institution further into political debates?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So today on—I’m simply going to refer you to the statement that I made on January 11.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not going to expand on it or repeat it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’m just not going to—this is really about the press conference and the economy and what we did today, but—and some ancillaries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I’m not going to be getting into that.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Can you say whether the Fed has responded to the subpoenas?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I have nothing for you on that today.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Mike.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Michael McKee from Bloomberg Radio TV.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Have you made a decision on whether you would remain as a Governor of the Federal Reserve, and, if so, would you tell us what it is?

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: And, if not, when might we anticipate a decision?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, and I really, once again, have nothing for you on that today—that either.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Why would you want to leave at all, under the circumstances?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, I don’t want to get into this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not something I’m—there’s a time and place for these questions, but not something I’m going to be getting into today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Claire.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Claire Jones, Financial Times.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thanks a lot for taking my questions—and another one that might lead to a similar answer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Give it a try.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: We’ve seen quite big movements in the dollar over recent days.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: What do you think is driving the U.S. currency lower?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: And have you been at all concerned just by the extent of the volatility we’ve seen this week?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, Claire, as you probably know, we don’t comment on the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Really, the Administration, and especially the Treasury Department, has the job of oversight over the currency and exchange rates and all of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t comment on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not our—not our role.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I have nothing for you.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: But, I mean, what’s your view on the market movements?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: I mean, what do you think’s behind them?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Is it asset managers diversifying?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Is it— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Yeah, I just don’t—we don’t talk about the dollar.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: We don’t talk about what moves it around.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: It’s just—it’s just not appropriate for us to do so.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Really, the Treasury Department has that—it’s their, their role, their bailiwick, and we stay off it.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: We do monetary policy and some other things, but we don’t—we don’t comment on the dollar.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Sorry.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Neil.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Neil Irwin with Axios.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Obviously no SEP in this meeting, but in light of the slight firming up of the language around growth in the labor market in the statement, should we assume that the timeline for any further rate cuts is pushed back, compared to what people might have thought in December?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, first of all, if you look at the incoming data since the last meeting, clear improvement in the outlook for growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The data have come in, and sentiment, the Beige Book—everything—comes in suggesting that this year starts off on a solid footing for growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation performed about as expected, and, as I mentioned, some of the labor market data came in suggesting evidence of stabilization.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s overall a stronger forecast, really, if that’s your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not sure I answered your question.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: But in terms of timing or pacing of any additional easing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we haven’t made—what we’d say about this was that after this meeting, after the three recent rate cuts, we’re well positioned to address the risks that we face on both sides of our dual mandate, and we’ll continue to make our decisions meeting by meeting based on the incoming data implications for—and the implications for the outlook and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Haven’t made any decisions about future meetings, but the economy is growing at a solid pace, the unemployment rate has been broadly stable, and inflation remains somewhat elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll be looking to our goal variables and letting the data light the way for us.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Steve.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Steve Liesman, CNBC.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And sticking with questions you might answer—thank you—you had previously, I believe, described the current policy rate being at the higher end of neutral.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And if you look at the longer run of the SEP and the longer-run rate, 16 of 19 officials are actually below there on their long run.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Is the Fed still in the process of bringing it down towards a middle range of neutral?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And what would it take to get there?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I—the count I did was that 4 of the 19 were at or above that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And maybe I missed by 1—I thought it was 4.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if you look at the dealer survey, it was 10 out of 58 were at or above.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re right, it’s the high—higher end of the range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we say is it’s within the range of plausible estimates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is the higher end of that range, but it’s—so for some people, I think, it’s neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think—and many of my colleagues think—it’s hard to look at the incoming data and say that policy’s significantly restrictive at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It may be—it may be sort of loosely neutral, or it may be somewhat restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s in the eye of the beholder, and, of course, no one knows with any precision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got a follow-up?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: I get what you’re saying, but I—some officials have described the Fed being in a mode of bringing it down eventually, over time.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Are you still in that mode, or is this a place to hang out?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, no, I would say, if you look at the SEP from December, you—most people had additional normalization.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But at the same time, we’ve done a lot of the process of normalizing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A good piece of it is done, with 75 basis points and, before that, 100.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s 175 basis points we’ve cut since we began cutting in September of 2024.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’ve moved now to 3 point—fed funds is running just a little below 3.65 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’ve moved a good way, and we think we’re well positioned here to watch how the economy performs, look at the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not making decisions about future meetings, but we do think we’re well positioned after those three cuts to let the data speak to us.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Amara.

speaker: AMARA OMEOKWE
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: AMARA OMEOKWE
sentence: Amara Omeokwe from Bloomberg News.

speaker: AMARA OMEOKWE
sentence: To what extent did the Committee discuss the possibility of cutting at this meeting or in March?

speaker: AMARA OMEOKWE
sentence: And how are you all thinking about the conditions that would merit another rate cut?

speaker: AMARA OMEOKWE
sentence: Is there broad agreement on the Committee about what it would take?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there was broad support on the Committee for holding today—“broad,” I would say, including among nonvoters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s where that was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, some people did want to cut and dissented.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the Committee [was] pretty broadly for holding today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not trying to articulate a test for what—for when to next cut, or whether to cut at the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we’re saying is, we’re well positioned as we make decisions meeting by meeting, looking at the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re in a position where we have to—we still have some tension between employment and inflation, but it’s less than it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that the upside risks to inflation and the downside risks to employment have probably both diminished a bit, so we’ll be looking at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s about how you weigh the risks to the two goals and how big those—and quantify them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so there are different views on the Committee, and we’ll find our way forward as the data evolve.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Edward.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Edward Lawrence from Fox Business.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Has the effects of tariffs already moved through the economy on prices?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A lot of it has.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, basically, there are many different estimates, and they’re all highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But most of the overrun in goods prices is from tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s actually good news, because if it weren’t from tariffs, it might mean it’s from demand, and that’s a harder problem to solve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do think tariffs are likely to move through and be a one-time price increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So most of the overshoot, if you were to take that out, you’d get—you would—I mean, inflation, core PCE inflation, is running just a bit above 2 percent ex the effects of tariffs on goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the other good news is if you look away from goods and look at services, you do see ongoing disinflation in all the categories of services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s a healthy development.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what’s going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The expectation is that we will see the effects of tariffs flowing through goods prices, peaking, and then starting to come down, assuming there are no new major tariff increases that are begun.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we expect to see over the course of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we see that—if we see that, that would be something that tells us that we can—we can loosen policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Also, if we see something that suggests that the labor market is not stabilizing, that in fact it’s—the downside risks reemerge, or the data just get worse, we’d have to look at both of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have a two-sided mandate.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: If I could—if President Trump does pick a new Fed Chairman before May, what does that look like?

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: How would you work with that person, and what does that transition period look like?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t have anything for you on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—that will depend on Congress’s actions and things I can’t speculate on.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Howard.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Howard Schneider with Reuters.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Thank you for taking our questions.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Given the changes in the statement and all you’ve said so far, is it fair to describe risks to your—to both sides of the mandate as roughly balanced right now?

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: And is the next move necessarily down?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’d say that the upside—again, the upside risks to inflation and the downside risks to employment have diminished.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But they still exist.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s still some tension between the mandates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Are they fully in balance?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we—again, we think our policy is in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ve just discussed reasons why we might change our policy, and we’ll just have to see how the data lead us.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: I’m wondering, a minute ago you said you felt expectations were consistent with your—with your mandate, that the 2- and the 10-year breakevens have moved quite notably in the last couple of weeks, I believe.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Is there any concern on that front?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I recently looked at all of the—both survey- and market-based short-term inflation expectations have come way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They were in a good place at the beginning of last year, they spiked around Liberation Day, and now they’ve fully retraced in the last few months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s very comforting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the longer term, inflation expectations have remained in places that are very consistent with 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So expectations are—have been solid, and they reflect confidence in the return to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Andrew.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Apologies if this is a little bit repetitive, but in the past you’ve said that the reason you cut rates was that the risk to the labor market was greater than the risk to the inflation side.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Is that still true?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We haven’t made—you’re right, we saw the labor market weakening, and we acted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think that was the appropriate thing to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have a—we will always act to address what we see as the economy moving away from our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Risks to both of the variables are a little less—I think that the upside risks to inflation, again, a little bit less, and the downside risks to employment a little less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I just would say that I’m not making a judgment about how one of them is more at risk than the other—just that the risks to both of them have diminished.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Okay.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: BIS wrote a paper last summer which concluded that global investors were hedging their dollar exposures, in ways that previously they hadn’t, because of policy uncertainty.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Do you agree with BIS?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We really don’t see much at all about that, that whole—that whole story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s just not a lot of data that suggests that there’s much to that.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Ana.

speaker: ANA SWANSON
sentence: Ana Swanson with the New York Times.

speaker: ANA SWANSON
sentence: Can you talk more about what you would need to see in the labor market to conclude it’s time to resume easing?

speaker: ANA SWANSON
sentence: Do you need to see further deterioration on the labor market, or would it be enough for inflation to soften?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll always be looking at both things, and so there could be combinations, infinite numbers of combinations, that would cause us to want to move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Certainly, a weakening labor market would be an argument for loosening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what’s happening with inflation?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If inflation were at the same time getting worse, you just have a very difficult situation there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll be looking at both.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Clearly, a weakening labor market calls for cutting; a stronger labor market says that the rates are in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll have to be making similar judgments, too, on inflation, though.

speaker: ANA SWANSON
sentence: And if inflation does pick back up and the labor market doesn’t show further signs of deterioration, is there a chance that you could raise rates, rather than simply remaining on hold?

speaker: ANA SWANSON
sentence: What would you need to see to consider hiking?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t take things off the table, but it isn’t anybody’s base case right now—anybody’s base case—that the next move will be a rate hike.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, ultimately, we’ll do what we think is the right thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s not where people’s expectations are right now.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Victoria.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Hi.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Victoria Guida with Politico.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: I wanted to ask, you’ve talked in the past about concerns about the U.S. fiscal trajectory, and we’ve seen in the Japanese bond market a lot of turmoil recently, in part due to concerns over their fiscal and long-term economic outlook.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: So do you worry that the U.S. could, at some point, find itself in a similar situation to Japan, whether for fiscal or demographic reasons?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over time, you’ve seen that U.S. rates have remained pretty—they haven’t moved a lot, really for a while.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But they haven’t moved a lot because of what’s been happening in Japan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s more of an “over time” thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The U.S. federal budget deficit is uncontroversially on an unsustainable path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The level of debt is not unsustainable—it’s very much sustainable—but the path is unsustainable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the sooner we work on it, the better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But right now we’re running a very large deficit at essentially full employment, and so the fiscal picture needs to be addressed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s not really being addressed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not in any way connecting it to some sort of near-term market event.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, ultimately, it’s something we’ll have to deal with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the end—in the endgame, that’s where you wind up is in some kind of a difficult thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s not where we are—it’s not where Japan is, either—but it’s certainly not where we are right now.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Does it reduce the effect of your rate cuts that longer-term rates have overall not really budged that much?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The thing is—I mean, technically, higher longer-term rates means less economic financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But remember—many, many things move longer-term rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not—and it’s not mostly what happens on the short end.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There can be effects of longer-term rates from our moving our policy around, but it’s much more assessments of the fiscal path, and fiscal policies, and risks and things like that that move the 10-year around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can look back and find periods where we’ve been very actively moving the policy rate over the course of a year, and over the course of that year, the 10-year is exactly where it started.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not—there’s not a tight link between 10-year rates and the overnight rate.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Elizabeth.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Thanks so much.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Elizabeth Schulze with ABC News.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who sits on the Senate Banking Committee, said he will block any Fed nominee, including the Chair, until this investigation into you is resolved.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Do you support this move by the senator, and what conversations have you had with the senator?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ve got nothing for you on that.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: More broadly, what would happen to American households if the Federal Reserve loses its ability to operate independent from politics?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, really, the point of independence is not to protect policymakers or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It just is that every advanced-economy democracy in the world has come around to this common practice.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just an institutional arrangement that is—that has served the people well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that is to have a separation between—to not have direct elected official control over the setting of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the reason is that monetary policy can be used through an election cycle to affect the economy in a way that will be politically worthwhile.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this isn’t—I’m not talking about the U.S. context, this is every advanced-economy democracy of any size.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a good practice, it’s pretty much everywhere among countries that look at all like the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think if you lose that, it’s—first of all, it would be hard to restore the credibility of the institution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If people lose their faith that we’re making decisions only on the basis of our assessment of what’s best for everyone, for the wide public, rather than trying to benefit one group or another—if you lose that, it’s going to be hard to retain it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we haven’t lost it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t believe we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I certainly hope we won’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s very important, and the reason it’s important is that it’s enabled central banks, generally, not to be perfect, but to serve the public well.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: You’re confident it can maintain that independence at this point?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I’m strongly committed to that, and so are my colleagues.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Archie.

speaker: ARCHIE HALL
sentence: Archie Hall from the Economist.

speaker: ARCHIE HALL
sentence: On that sort of stabilization of the labor market question, how much do you see the weakening we saw over the past six months, year, as a kind of data mirage around immigration, the government shutdown, and so on, that’s now resolved?

speaker: ARCHIE HALL
sentence: Or how much have we seen a kind of real underlying firming up in the state of the labor market, do you think?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, part of it is, to your point, part of it just is that, that labor supply—growth in labor supply has come to essentially a halt from a fairly fast clip of growth over the last couple of years driven by immigration, and then the halt being driven by a very sudden stop in immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, many outcomes were possible with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Supply came way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It turns out that demand for labor also came down a very similar amount, maybe just a little bit more, which is why the unemployment rate has gone up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t know whether that’s a coincidence or not, but that’s what’s happened with that part.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if you look at other things, like, for example, the—just to pick a couple—the Conference Board’s measure of job availability that came out, I don’t know, was it yesterday or today?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it shows—it’s a survey showing that workers feel like job availability is—it’s a very low reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Just one reading, but it’s an indication of softening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People—part-time for economic reasons, which is a category within the broader U-6 category measure, has moved up significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there are lots of—and I could go on and on—there are lots of little places that suggest that the labor market has softened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But part of—but you’re right, part of payroll job softening is that both the supply and demand for labor has, has come down—growth in those two have come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that makes it a difficult time to read the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So imagine they both came down a lot, to the point where there is no job growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Is that full employment?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In a sense it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If demand and supply are in—are in balance, you could say that’s full employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, is it—do we really feel like that’s, that’s a maximum-employment economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a challenging—it’s a very challenging and quite unusual situation.

speaker: ARCHIE HALL
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: ARCHIE HALL
sentence: And one more—on growth and the kind of strong growth outlook or strengthening growth outlook you’re now seeing, how much of that is the fiscal stimulus we’re seeing from the Beautiful Bill, the tax cuts, and all that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re seeing it already.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You don’t have much of a fiscal—I think the outlook, you’re right, it’s financial conditions and it’s fiscal policy for ’26.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you’ve got strong consumption that’s been happening before financial conditions have been supportive but before the fiscal effects really are shown.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So essentially the economy has, once again, surprised us with its strength—not for the first time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumer spending, although it’s, it’s uneven across income categories, but consumer spending overall numbers are good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re benefiting from the—from the AI buildout of data centers—that’s another thing we’re benefiting from.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the economy, overall, growth is—growth is on solid footing, it looks like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s not just those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just that consumers—the consumer is filling out surveys that sound really negative and then spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s been a disconnect for some time between downbeat surveys and reasonably good spending data.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Christine.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: Thanks, Chair Powell.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: Christine Romans from NBC News.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: You talked about how consumer spending is uneven.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: The President calls inflation “defeated” and “solved.” The FOMC says it’s a “somewhat elevated” inflation.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: But you talked about those customer survey—or those consumer sentiment surveys and public opinion polls that show that most families say the cost of living is still issue number one.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: What is the conversation around the table with your colleagues about how wealthier consumers seem to be driving so much of the economy, and why so many families still feel like they just can’t make ends meet after five years of rising prices?

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: What is that discussion like?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So a couple things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One, there’s something, something to it in that we know that higher-income households tend to own real estate and tend to own stocks, stocks and securities, and those assets have been going up in value, and increases in wealth do support spending over time, so—and that’s clearly a part of the story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also know that for some time now, for a year or more, we’ve been hearing from retailers, for example, that serve lower-income customers, whether it be food or the big-box stores or any—they’re saying the same thing, which is, “Our consumers are looking to economize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re trading down from brands, and they’re buying less and changing their buying habits and that kind of thing.” So we’re seeing that, and that’s—that is a reality of what we’re seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re still consuming, but they’re feeling it in a different way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say more broadly, on affordability, we have a vast network through the Reserve Banks, and also through the Board of Governors, where we talk to small and large businesses and households.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we do hear a lot about affordability, and we take—we take that very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we take it to heart because our job is—one of our jobs is price stability, and so the best thing we can do for people who are feeling that squeeze is to keep inflation under control and, frankly, to finish the job of getting inflation back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: You mentioned the AI buildout as being positive for economic growth this year.

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: I wonder as you look at the weakest year—last year—for job creation of a nonrecession year since, like, 2003, are you concerned about AI maybe supplanting more entry-level work and entry-level jobs?

speaker: CHRISTINE ROMANS
sentence: And how does that play into your—what you’re watching about the labor market?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So everyone, of course, is watching AI and the deployment and trying to understand exactly what’s happening, and there’s a wide range of possibilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s hard to say, and of course anyone who uses it is amazed at what it can accomplish, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So every technological wave will eliminate some jobs and create other jobs, and it’s always been the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look back, wave after wave after wave, there will be some disruption, but ultimately technology increases productivity, which is the basis for rising wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it may not all happen immediately, but over time it’s what—it’s what enables incomes to rise over time is rising productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we always ask, well this is going to be different, is it going to be different?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we may, in any case, see, in the short term, jobs that are being eliminated by the capabilities of AI.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We may see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just don’t know what the overall effect is going to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So how to think about it—in macroeconomic terms, it’s very hard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can look at the aggregate data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can analyze, for example—there is some connection, it appears, between the low hiring rate for recent college grads and AI, but it’s not the main, or only, driver.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You hear large companies, though, saying—many of them saying—that they either won’t be hiring for some time, or that they’re hiring less, or that they’re laying people off, and they tend to refer to AI when they do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re all watching and learning, and it could—it could certainly have pretty significant effects on the economy, the workforce, and our society.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t really have the tools to address the concerns that may arise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we have a lot of people who focus on analyzing it and try to—try to understand what the macroeconomic implications are, which is our job.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Beiyi.

speaker: BEIYI SEOW
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: BEIYI SEOW
sentence: Beiyi from AFP News Agency.

speaker: BEIYI SEOW
sentence: You mentioned earlier that on inflation, the broad expectation was for a one-time price increase and then for inflation to come down.

speaker: BEIYI SEOW
sentence: I was wondering, is your expectation still for inflation to start cooling in the second half of 2026?

speaker: BEIYI SEOW
sentence: And if you could elaborate how far we are from target currently.

speaker: BEIYI SEOW
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So how far we are from target is, as I mentioned in my opening remarks, we’re—we had 3 percent—3.0 percent core PCE inflation over the 12 months ending in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s pretty much what we had the year before.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, on net, no progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the story behind that is modestly positive in that most of the overshoot was in goods prices, which we think is related to tariffs, and ultimately we think those will not result in inflation, as opposed to a one-time price increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Okay, so that’s where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of, you asked—so no one thinks they will, ex ante, understand really clearly, precisely when this will happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But there’s an expectation that sometime in the middle quarters of the year, we’ll see tariff inflation topping out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what we do is, we—when a tariff is put in place, we track the effect of those tariffs over a six-, seven-, eight-, nine-month period, and you can see—and then you can see for that tariff how long it takes to reach a place where it’s affected the price level and that’s it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re getting better at that, and our estimate is that it’ll be sometime in the middle of the year, but I wouldn’t look for great precision in that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’ll be able to see whether things are moving in that direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’ll be able to see.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Richard Escobedo.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: Thanks, Chair Powell.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: I’m Richard Escobedo with CBS News.

speaker: RICHARD ESCOBEDO
sentence: I want to look outside the U.S. about what’s happening outside our shores and how it impacts the U.S. Canada’s prime minister said last week that there’s been a “rupture in the global order,” and I wonder how you’re thinking about geopolitical risk as it relates to the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I can’t—I can’t comment on that speech or statement or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Geopolitical risk for us is—a lot of it is around energy, oil.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so far we haven’t—for all the turmoil, we really—oil prices have come down, as you know, and so we don’t really see much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Longer than that, it’s trade, and the trade—the economy—our economy has pulled through pretty well, you’d have to say, given the very significant changes in trade policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The U.S. economy has, has pushed right through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Partly that is—that the way that what was implemented was significantly less than what was announced at the beginning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, other countries didn’t retaliate, and, in addition, a good part of it hasn’t been passed through to consumers yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s being—it’s being taken by companies that stand between the consumer and the exporter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s where that is.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jennifer.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Jennifer Schonberger with Yahoo Finance.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: With third-quarter GDP growing at 4.4 percent and the fourth quarter expected to have a five handle on it, as to what the Atlanta Fed is predicting, at a time when you had a government shutdown and we thought that was going to shave off some growth.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: You’ve also got the fiscal tailwinds, you’ve talked about big tax refunds coming, potential tariff dividend.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: How could you cut rates and not spur inflation in that environment?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, we didn’t cut rates today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it depends on how fast potential output is growing, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m just asking in principle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not—I’m not saying this is what’s happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s growth, and there’s how fast the potential is growing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And in a time of high productivity growth, potential output is rising.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it really matters whether potential output is growing as fast as actual output.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it would matter over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The numbers you cite were for quarters, and quarterly GDP is—you need to look at 12 months, because quarterly GDP can be very lumpy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Quarterly GDP [growth] was negative in the first quarter last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the overall—over the year, the numbers were nothing like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was more in the mid-2s for the year.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: And how do you explain the divide right now between strong economic growth and the job market?

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Is it productivity that’s filling the gap?

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: And is productivity being driven by AI at this point?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we—there has—you’re right, there has been a divide of solid growth but what looked like a weakening labor market, and that can be explained by rising productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would say we do see signs, certainly, of the unemployment rate stabilizing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it may be we’re seeing the beginning of the resolution of those two things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Also, as you probably know, the lore is that when GDP and the labor market get into an argument, in the end, labor market is more—the labor market data is more reliable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP data is very hard to collect and understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, nonetheless, I think we may be seeing that tension resolving a little bit—too soon to say with any confidence, though.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Matt Egan.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Matt Egan with CNN.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Chair Powell, after today you have two meetings left as Fed Chair.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: You’ve obviously experienced a lot during your time as Fed Chair, served under multiple Presidents.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: I’m wondering what advice you have for whoever your successor might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Honestly, I’d say a couple things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One is stay out of elected politics.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Don’t get pulled into elected politics.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Don’t do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s another thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Another is that our window into democratic accountability is Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s not a passive burden for us to go to Congress and talk to people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s an affirmative, regular obligation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you want democratic legitimacy, you earn it by your interactions with our elected overseers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so it’s something you need to work hard at, and I have worked hard at it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the last thing is, it’s easy to—it’s easy to criticize government institutions in so many ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will tell whoever it is, you’re about to meet the most qualified group of people you not only have ever worked with [but also that] you will ever work with, when you meet Fed staff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And not everybody’s perfect, but there isn’t a better cadre of professionals more dedicated to the public well-being than work at the Fed.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Thanks for that answer.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: If I may follow up—as I’m sure you’ve noticed, gold and silver prices have experienced historic gains of late.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: And I’m wondering how much attention, if any, you pay to those moves, and what message you may take from these significant price increases we’ve seen for precious metals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Don’t take much message macroeconomically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The argument can be made that we’re losing credibility or something—it’s simply not the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look—if you look at where inflation expectations are, our credibility is right where it needs to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look at those things, we don’t get spun up over particular asset price changes, although we do monitor them, of course.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nicole for the last question.

speaker: NICOLE GOODKIND
sentence: Hi.

speaker: NICOLE GOODKIND
sentence: Nicole Goodkind, Barron’s.

speaker: NICOLE GOODKIND
sentence: Some prominent critics have charged that the Fed’s economic models are somewhat backward looking but should be more forward looking, incorporating things like productivity increases from AI.

speaker: NICOLE GOODKIND
sentence: How do you incorporate current and future developments into your analysis and decisionmaking, and do you have an answer to those critics?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so by and large, those criticisms, as somebody on the inside—they just don’t make sense, and I’ll tell you why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Every FOMC participant writes down a forecast every quarter, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Summary of Economic Projections.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s the basis for how we think about the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the other thing is, what an economic model can do is it can grind up all the data for the last number of years, 50 years let’s say, and it can—it can identify what are the relationships between variables A, B, C, D, and all that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it can tell you if you change one of those variables, this is what should happen in the macroeconomy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s just the way it works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: However, the structure of the macroeconomy is constantly changing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For example, we hadn’t had a pandemic in 100 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It wasn’t in the model.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we knew it from the very beginning—it was not in the model.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A trade war of this scope—we’d never had that in 100 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so there’s great uncertainty at different points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Another thing I’ll say is, when it comes to technological developments that raise potential output, some kind of technological revolution like happened in the ’90s here and like may be happening now with AI—we’re all over that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everyone studies those periods, and we’re very clear-eyed about the possibility that this higher productivity may persist, and also that it may not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not—no one’s sitting here unaware of the possibility of higher productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve been talking about it for three years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It long predates the current situation—it’s been going on for five or six years we’ve had productivity higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve been talking about it that whole time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s very much on our minds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we are well aware that higher productivity means higher potential output, and it changes the way you think about, potentially, inflation growth, labor market, and all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s all in our models.

speaker: NICOLE GOODKIND
sentence: And just a quick follow-up: We’ve been talking a lot about tariffs passing through, and we’ve been talking a lot about them for the past few months.

speaker: NICOLE GOODKIND
sentence: The trade landscape is still in a constant state of flux.

speaker: NICOLE GOODKIND
sentence: Announcements, threats, negotiations—they’re all frequently changing.

speaker: NICOLE GOODKIND
sentence: So I’m wondering how you actually track these.

speaker: NICOLE GOODKIND
sentence: How—what data or channels are most critical to follow this in real time?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Trade?

speaker: NICOLE GOODKIND
sentence: Yeah, the impact of tariffs and how they’re changing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, I think our staff has done a really nice job on that, and they kind of put it together in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So as I mentioned, a tariff gets put in place, you can pretty much track its effects on pricing and on everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so you build a model up from all of the—all of the tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the beginning, it was very much of a forecast; now, it’s—every, every cycle that goes by, it becomes more informed by actual data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we were—we—our forecasts were not far off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What changed was, as I think I said earlier, what changed was what was implemented was smaller than what was announced.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, we didn’t see retaliation internationally, and I think people did generally expect that because we saw that in the past.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that really mattered too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then the other thing is the pass-through—didn’t know how fast that was going to be to consumers, didn’t know how much exporters would take, how much companies in the middle would take, and how much the consumer would take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it turns out it’s a lot of companies in the middle—who, by the way, are pretty strongly committed to passing the rest of it through, which is one of the reasons why we need to keep our eye on inflation and not declare victory prematurely.
